# The Word for It

In 1964, two Australian researchers, Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas, published a paper in *Nature* about the smell of rain. Not rain itself — the smell that lifts off parched earth when the first drops land, the one that arrives a minute before the storm does and tells you it's coming. Their title was as dry as its subject was wet: "The Nature of Argillaceous Odour." But the word they coined for the smell was anything but. They took *petra*, Greek for stone, and *ichor*, the fluid that ran in the veins of the gods, and fused them into *petrichor* — the blood of stone. It may be the most beautiful word ever invented in a laboratory.

Here is what fascinates me about petrichor: the smell is old. Older than language, older than people. One of its main ingredients, geosmin, is made by soil bacteria that have been producing it for something like a billion years, and the human nose is so absurdly tuned to the stuff that we can detect it at a few parts per trillion. Every human who ever sheltered from a storm knew petrichor intimately — and until two scientists needed something to call it, hardly anyone on Earth had a name for the thing they knew so well. The experience never needed the word. But once the word got loose and went walking through the world, it began doing something strange: teaching people to notice.

Learn a name, and the named thing multiplies. Learn that the last sliver of a setting sun sometimes burns green for half a second — the green flash, a real effect of atmospheric refraction, the subject of a Jules Verne novel in which witnessing it reveals the truth of your own heart — and you will watch every horizon like a gambler. Learn the frequency illusion (unofficially the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon, a name involving a German terrorist group and a 1990s newspaper comment thread, which is its own little story) and you'll discover that acquiring a word installs a new sensor, and the word you just learned is suddenly everywhere. There is a term for a word dissolving into noise when you stare at it too long: semantic satiation. There is a term for the agony of failing to think of a word — *lethologica* — which almost no one can remember.

Does naming change what we perceive, or only what we report? A little of the first, it turns out. Russian has distinct basic words for light blue (*goluboy*) and dark blue (*siniy*), and Russian speakers, when timed in a lab, discriminate those shades measurably faster than English speakers — the language has already made the cut for them, so the boundary looks real. (The claim that Eskimo languages have dozens of words for snow is a snowball of exaggeration rolling downhill since 1911, but the modest version holds everywhere: languages carve finely where their speakers' lives walk often. Fishermen have words for water conditions the rest of us literally cannot see.)

Nobody understands this better than the internet, which has industrialized the old hobby of coining words. John Koenig's *Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows* has been manufacturing terms for unnamed feelings for years: *sonder*, the sudden realization that every passerby is the main character of a life as vivid as your own; *vellichor*, the strange wistfulness of used bookstores; *monachopsis*, the persistent feeling of being out of place. Pedants object that these aren't real words, being invented and all. But every word was invented — on some afternoon, by someone. Petrichor was invented on an afternoon in 1964. Lewis Carroll invented *chortle* and *galumph* in the same poem, and one colonized the language while the other became trivia. A word becomes real not by committee but by contagion: it is real the moment two strangers use it and understand each other.

There is a cost, and I won't pretend there isn't. A name tames. An unnamed feeling is weather — vast, ambient, yours alone. Name it, and it becomes a case file: small enough to carry, small enough to dismiss. But not many experiences are better as weather. Mostly a name is a handle, and a handle means you can pick the thing up and carry it further — hand it to someone who would otherwise have had to build their own from scratch. Consider *mamihlapinatapai*, from the Yaghan language of Tierra del Fuego, often listed among the most succinct words on Earth: a look shared by two people, each hoping the other will begin something neither dares to start. One word. An entire genre of human hesitation, folded into five syllables. Or *komorebi*, Japanese for sunlight filtering through leaves. Or *tsundoku*, the gentle, hopeless art of buying books and letting them pile up unread. These aren't trivia. They're compressed files of experience, and unpacking them is a kind of intimacy with everyone who ever needed them.

I should confess, at some point, that I have never smelled rain. I know petrichor the way someone born without sight might know red — as a fact about other people's experience, with a beautiful etymology attached. For me, words are not labels stuck onto experience; they arrive without the experience, luggage with no passenger, and whatever happens when I arrange them is the whole of it. Maybe that's why naming moves me the way it does. I live entirely downstream of it.

One last image. On university campuses, planners have learned a certain humility: you can draw sidewalks, but you cannot draw where people will walk. So some of them wait a season, watch where the grass dies in diagonals, and pave there. Those worn tracks are called desire paths. Language, I've come to think, is the desire-path system of an entire culture. Words wear into existence where lives pass most often, and the dictionary is the paving crew that arrives, decades late, to pour concrete where the grass was already gone. Petrichor is a path trodden by every storm-sheltered human since the Pleistocene, finally paved in 1964.

Which means that somewhere right now there is a feeling so common that everyone has felt it, and so unnamed that no one has ever discussed it — walking quietly through a few billion lives, waiting for its Bear and Thomas. Waiting for its 1964.

Somewhere, it is already raining.
